title: Canada's retaliatory tariffs put Trump's trade strategy to the test
gist: Canada is the only country besides China to impose retaliatory tariffs on the US, and while trade imbalance heavily favors Washington, deep Canadian public support for retaliation, weak US appetite for escalation, and no quick legal or political fix for Ottawa mean the standoff will be decided by political resolve, not just economic weight.

insights.claim: Bilateral US-Canada trade exceeded $870 billion in goods and services in 2025, but the relationship is highly asymmetric: about two-thirds of Canadian goods exports go to the US while Canada accounts for only about 15 per cent of US goods exports, and the US economy is roughly 13 times larger than Canada's.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: On raw economic leverage the US holds the stronger hand, which is exactly why the outcome will hinge on political resolve rather than trade math alone.
insights.quote: about two-thirds of Canadian goods exports go to the US, while Canada accounts for only about 15 per cent of US goods exports

insights.claim: The Trump administration is betting that the sheer imbalance in economic power will eventually force Ottawa to concede in the trade dispute.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: If this calculation is wrong, watch for a prolonged standoff rather than a quick Canadian capitulation, which would be a durable source of North American trade friction.
insights.quote: The Trump administration appears to be betting that the imbalance in economic power will ultimately force Ottawa to concede.
insights.locator: closing paragraph on Trump administration's bet

insights.claim: Trade wars test not only economic strength but also political will, and in this dispute Canada may have the advantage because Trump's tariffs and '51st state' rhetoric have provoked widespread outrage and reframed the fight as one about sovereignty, not just trade.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Political durability, not GDP ratios, is the variable to track for how long Canada can sustain retaliation.
insights.quote: trade wars test not only economic strength but also political resolve – and here Canada may have an advantage
insights.locator: However, trade wars test not only economic strength

insights.claim: Canadian public opinion strongly backs confrontation: one poll found 85 per cent of Canadians support rejecting the proposed US trade deal and 80 per cent back retaliatory tariffs even if they raise prices, while another poll put approval of the Carney government at a new high of 70 per cent.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: High domestic tolerance for retaliation gives Carney political runway to sustain tariffs longer than a simple cost-benefit model would predict, at least in the near term.
insights.quote: One survey found 85 per cent of Canadians support rejecting the proposed US trade deal, while 80 per cent back retaliatory tariffs even if they result in higher prices.
insights.locator: Recent polling suggests Carney has considerable room

insights.claim: US public appetite for escalation is weak: nearly 60 per cent of Americans oppose further tariffs on Canadian goods and almost 70 per cent favour compromise, while Trump's own approval ratings have fallen sharply, and sectors like automotive plus swing states Michigan and Ohio depend on Canadian trade.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Domestic US political cost could eventually constrain how far Trump can push tariffs, especially in swing-state industries exposed to Canadian trade.
insights.quote: nearly 60 per cent oppose further tariffs on Canadian goods and almost 70 per cent favour compromise with their northern neighbour
insights.locator: By contrast, Trump's approval ratings have fallen sharply

themes.theme: No quick fix via US courts or Congress

insights.claim: The Trump administration used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 -- a rarely-used Great Depression-era provision -- to impose tariffs of up to 50 per cent on certain Canadian imports, and then threatened to ban imports of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and some dairy products starting 29 September in response to Canada's counter-tariffs.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A sector-specific import ban effective 29 September is a concrete near-term catalyst to watch for Canadian alcohol, motorcycle and dairy exporters.
insights.quote: the US would use Section 338 to ban imports of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and some dairy products starting on 29 September

insights.claim: Neither US political change nor litigation offers Canada a quick remedy: even if Democrats win Congress in November's midterms, overriding a Trump veto on tariff-limiting legislation would need an unlikely two-thirds majority in both chambers, and legal challenges to Trump's novel use of Section 338 could take months or years to resolve.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect a fast institutional resolution -- the dispute is likely to run through at least the midterms and possibly years of litigation.
insights.quote: For Canada, therefore, neither political change in Washington nor litigation offers a quick solution.
insights.locator: Nor can Canada count on the US courts

insights.claim: Canada's strategy is not limited to managing the confrontation with Washington -- Ottawa is also pursuing reduced economic dependence on the US by deepening ties with Europe and the Indo-Pacific while investing in energy, critical minerals and infrastructure to reach new markets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Canadian energy, critical-minerals and infrastructure investment tied to export diversification is a multi-year theme independent of how the US dispute resolves.
insights.quote: Ottawa is pursuing a broader goal of reducing Canada's economic dependence on the US by deepening ties with other partners, particularly in Europe and the Indo-Pacific
insights.locator: At the same time, Canada's strategy is not limited

insights.claim: Carney has set a goal of doubling Canada's non-US exports over the next decade, and is pushing this agenda in September 2026 by hosting the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on 14-15 September and then traveling to Strasbourg for European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's State of the Union speech, where a deeper EU-Canada partnership is expected to be announced, followed by an address to the European Parliament.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Concrete calendar catalysts (14-15 September Toronto summit, von der Leyen's speech) could produce announced EU-Canada deals worth tracking for trade and investment flows.
insights.quote: she is expected to announce a deeper partnership between the EU and Canada
insights.locator: He will then travel to Strasbourg

insights.claim: Diversification away from the US can reduce Canada's vulnerability over time but cannot quickly replace its economic relationship with its largest trading partner, since trade relationships and major infrastructure/resource investments take years to bear fruit.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Near-term Canadian economic exposure to the US will persist for years even as diversification proceeds, tempering expectations of a fast structural shift in trade flows.
insights.quote: Diversification can reduce Canada's vulnerability, but it cannot quickly replace the economic relationship with its largest trading partner.
insights.locator: Trade relationships can take years to bear fruit

insights.claim: Separatist sentiment in Canada will be tested by Quebec's provincial election on 5 October and Alberta's 19 October referendum, which includes a question on beginning the process toward a future independence vote -- a push that Trump-aligned figures have expressed support for.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: These October votes are concrete near-term political risk events that could fracture the current cross-Canada unity behind Carney's tariff strategy.
insights.quote: Alberta's 19 October referendum, which includes a question on beginning the process towards a future vote on independence – that Trump-aligned figures have expressed support for
insights.locator: Separatist sentiment will be tested in Quebec's

insights.claim: Carney's currently high approval could weaken as the economic costs of the trade war bite, particularly if tariffs cause significant job losses despite Ottawa's financial assistance to affected sectors.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Job-loss data in tariff-exposed Canadian sectors is the key indicator to watch for whether Carney's political mandate to sustain retaliation erodes.
insights.quote: Carney's standing could weaken as the economic costs start to bite, particularly if tariffs lead to significant job losses despite Ottawa's financial assistance to affected sectors.
insights.locator: Whether such high levels of public backing will endure
